sections.title: Derive parallel-plate capacitance
sections.search:
## Capacitors: first decide what stays fixed

A capacitor stores energy in an electric field between conductors. Its plates carry +Q and −Q. In $C = \frac{Q}{V}$, Q is the magnitude on ONE plate, not the algebraic total charge of the pair. One farad is one coulomb per volt. Use $\mathrm{\mu F} = 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F}$, $\mathrm{nF} = 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{F}$, and $\mathrm{pF} = 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F}$.

$$C=Q/V,\quad Q=CV,\quad V=Q/C.$$

For a linear ideal capacitor, geometry and dielectric determine C. A larger Q does not automatically mean a larger C: the applied voltage can increase in the same proportion. Capacitive keyboard keys exploit smaller separation increasing capacitance.

Derive parallel-plate capacitance

For large parallel plates with edge effects neglected, $\sigma = \frac{Q}{A}$ and $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}$. The approximately uniform gap field gives $V = Ed$. Substitute:

$$V=\frac{Qd}{\epsilon A}\Rightarrow C=\frac QV=\frac{\epsilon A}{d}=\frac{\kappa\epsilon_0 A}{d}.$$

Here $\varepsilon_{0} \approx 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\,\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{m}}$ and $\kappa$ is a dimensionless dielectric constant. Rearrangements are $A = \frac{Cd}{\left( \kappa \varepsilon_{0} \right)}$, $d = \frac{\kappa \varepsilon_{0} A}{C}$, $\kappa = \frac{Cd}{\left( \varepsilon_{0} A \right)}$. The parallel-plate model needs plate dimensions much larger than gap d. Do not use the same equation for arbitrary conductor shapes.

**Worked example — primary p. 14.** $C = 1.0\,\mathrm{F}$, $d = 1.0\,\mathrm{mm}$ in vacuum gives $A = \frac{1 \times 0.001}{\left( 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \right)} = 1.13 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$. A missing milli prefix changes the answer by 1000.

**Worked example — primary p. 14.** $A = 2.0\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$, $d = 5.0\,\mathrm{mm}$, and $V = 10{,}000\,\mathrm{V}$ give $C = 3.54 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{F} = 0.00354\,\mathrm{\mu F}$, $Q = 35.4\,\mathrm{\mu C}$, and $E = 2.0 \times 10^{6}\,\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{m}}$. Check $Q = CV$ and $V = Ed$ independently.

sections.title: Dielectrics: connected versus disconnected battery
sections.search:
Dielectrics: connected versus disconnected battery

A dielectric polarizes and increases capacitance when it fills the gap: $C_{\mathrm{new}} = \kappa C_{\mathrm{old}}$. It can mechanically separate plates and permit greater voltage before breakdown, depending on the material and conditions.

| Quantity | Battery stays connected | Battery is disconnected, ideal isolated capacitor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Voltage | Fixed by ideal battery | Divides by $\kappa$ |
| Free charge magnitude | Multiplies by $\kappa$ | Fixed |
| Capacitance | Multiplies by $\kappa$ | Multiplies by $\kappa$ |
| Field in fully filled fixed gap | Fixed | Divides by $\kappa$ |
| Stored energy | Multiplies by $\kappa$ | Divides by $\kappa$ |

**Derive these changes.** Start with $Q = CV$. Fix V in the connected case or Q in the isolated case. Then use $U = \frac{CV^{2}}{2}$ or $\frac{Q^{2}}{\left( 2\,\mathrm{C} \right)}$. The connected capacitor can gain stored energy because the battery exchanges energy and charge. The isolated capacitor's energy decrease can become mechanical work during dielectric insertion.

**Extensions — partial dielectric geometry.** Two materials occupying side-by-side area fractions share the voltage, so $C = \frac{\varepsilon_{0} \left( \kappa_{1} A_{1} + \kappa_{2} A_{2} \right)}{d}$. Layers stacked across the gap share the series charge, so $\frac{1}{C} = \frac{d_{1}}{\left( \kappa_{1} \varepsilon_{0} A \right)} + \frac{d_{2}}{\left( \kappa_{2} \varepsilon_{0} A \right)}$. Use the geometry to choose the connection model.

sections.title: Derive all three energy expressions
sections.search:
Derive all three energy expressions

The voltage rises while charging. An additional dq requires work $dU = V \left( q \right) dq = \left( \frac{q}{C} \right) dq$. Integrate from zero to Q:

$$U=\int_0^Q\frac qC\,dq=\frac{Q^2}{2C}=\frac12QV=\frac12CV^2.$$

Multiplying the FINAL voltage by the entire charge gives QV, twice the stored energy. A linear voltage rise has average charging voltage $\frac{V}{2}$. Rearranging gives $V = \sqrt{\left( \frac{2 U}{C} \right)}$, $C = \frac{2 U}{V^{2}}$, or $Q = \sqrt{\left( 2 CU \right)}$, with magnitudes and physically positive C.

**Worked example — primary p. 16.** $C = 5.80\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ and $V = 400\,\mathrm{V}$ give $U = 0.5 \left( 5.80 \times 10^{-6} \right) \left( 400^{2} \right) = 0.464\,\mathrm{J}$. The answer fixes the exponent obscured in some PDF text extraction. A $5.0\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ capacitor at $1.5\,\mathrm{V}$ has $Q = 7.5\,\mathrm{\mu C}$.

Substitute $C = \frac{\varepsilon A}{d}$ and $V = Ed$: $U = \frac{\varepsilon E^{2} Ad}{2}$. Divide by gap volume Ad to derive field-energy density $u = \frac{\varepsilon E^{2}}{2}$ for a linear material.

sections.title: Networks: derive series and parallel rules
sections.search:
Networks: derive series and parallel rules

Parallel branches share the SAME two nodes. Their voltages are equal and terminal charges add: $Q_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum C_{i} V$. Thus $C_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum C_{i}$. Series capacitors in an initially uncharged isolated-intermediate-node chain carry equal charge magnitude. Their voltage drops add: $V_{\mathrm{tot}} = Q\sum \left( \frac{1}{C_{i}} \right)$, so $\frac1{C_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\sum_i\frac1{C_i}$.

For two series capacitors, $C_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{C_{1} C_{2}}{\left( C_{1} + C_{2} \right)}$. Solving for an unknown gives $C_{2} = \frac{C_{\mathrm{eq}}C_{1}}{\left( C_{1} - C_{\mathrm{eq}} \right)}$, requiring $C_{1} > C_{\mathrm{eq}} > 0$. In parallel, $C_{2} = C_{\mathrm{eq}} - C_{1} > 0$. Series equivalent capacitance is smaller than the smallest element; parallel equivalent capacitance exceeds each positive element.

**Worked example — primary p. 24.** Connect $6\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ and $3\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ to $18\,\mathrm{V}$. Series: $C_{\mathrm{eq}} = 2\,\mathrm{\mu F}$, $Q_{\mathrm{each}} = 36\,\mathrm{\mu C}$, $V_{6} = 6\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_{3} = 12\,\mathrm{V}$. Parallel: $C_{\mathrm{eq}} = 9\,\mathrm{\mu F}$, $V_{\mathrm{each}} = 18\,\mathrm{V}$, $Q_{6} = 108\,\mathrm{\mu C}$, $Q_{3} = 54\,\mathrm{\mu C}$. The smaller SERIES capacitor has the larger voltage because its charge magnitude is the same.

For a mixed network, label nodes before reducing it. Two nearby symbols are not necessarily parallel. Reduce a valid group, record its equivalent value, solve the terminal circuit, and then work backward. Use the original group’s shared Q or shared V to recover each element. Check ΣVi for series groups and ΣQi for parallel groups.

**Worked extension — reduce, then restore the branches.** Put $2\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ and $4\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ in parallel. Connect that group in series with $3\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ across $12\,\mathrm{V}$. The parallel group is $6\,\mathrm{\mu F}$. Its series equivalent with $3\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ is $\frac{\left( 6 \times 3 \right)}{\left( 6 + 3 \right)} = 2\,\mathrm{\mu F}$. The source transfers $Q = 2 \times 12 = 24\,\mathrm{\mu C}$ to each series unit.

The $6\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ group has voltage $\frac{24}{6} = 4\,\mathrm{V}$. The $3\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ capacitor has voltage $\frac{24}{3} = 8\,\mathrm{V}$. Both parallel capacitors share $4\,\mathrm{V}$, so their charges are $8\,\mathrm{\mu C}$ and $16\,\mathrm{\mu C}$. Their sum is the group's $24\,\mathrm{\mu C}$. Check energy: $\tfrac{1}{2} \left( 2\,\mathrm{\mu F} \right) \left( 12^{2} \right) = 144\,\mathrm{\mu J}$. The individual energies are 16, 32, and $96\,\mathrm{\mu J}$, which also sum to $144\,\mathrm{\mu J}$. A single equivalent capacitance alone does not reveal every branch voltage.

**Charge-sharing extension.** Disconnect two capacitors from their supplies and join their positive plates together. With no leakage, $V_{f} = \frac{\left( C_{1} V_{1} + C_{2} V_{2} \right)}{\left( C_{1} + C_{2} \right)}$. Reverse one capacitor's polarity by using a negative signed initial voltage. Final energy need not equal the sum of initial capacitor energies; the connection can dissipate energy. Charge conservation does not imply capacitor-energy conservation.

For $C_{1} = 2\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ at $12\,\mathrm{V}$ and $C_{2} = 4\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ at $0\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_{f} = 4\,\mathrm{V}$. Initial stored energy is $144\,\mathrm{\mu J}$; final energy is $48\,\mathrm{\mu J}$. The difference, $96\,\mathrm{\mu J}$, leaves the capacitor fields during the transient. Real connections transfer it through resistance, radiation, or other losses. An ideal zero-resistance instantaneous connection is not a complete transient model.

Derive capacitance with the charge, geometry, and units visible

:::derivation From the plate fields to $C = \frac{\varepsilon A}{d}$
**Sources:** Primary pp. 7–13; companion pp. 1–4. Use large parallel plates, a uniform linear dielectric, and negligible edge effects.

1. Write the free surface-charge density as $\sigma = \frac{Q}{A}$.
2. Add the two ideal plate fields. The gap field is $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}$, not $\frac{\sigma}{\left( 2 \varepsilon \right)}$.
3. Use the uniform-gap potential difference magnitude $V = Ed$.
4. Substitute $\sigma = \frac{Q}{A}$ to obtain $V = \frac{Qd}{\left( \varepsilon A \right)}$.
5. Divide charge by voltage: $C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{\varepsilon A}{d}$.

**Unit check.** $\frac{\varepsilon A}{d}$ has units $\frac{\left( \frac{F}{m} \right) \left( m^{2} \right)}{m} = F$. The dielectric constant $\kappa = \frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_{0}}$ has no unit. Do not confuse $\kappa$ with Coulomb's constant k.
:::

{{figure:m6-main:12|The primary dielectric-constant table at 20°C, also reproduced in the companion.}}

The table gives $\kappa = 1$ for vacuum and about 1.00059 for air at $1\,\mathrm{atm}$. The usual classroom approximation uses air ≈ vacuum. Listed examples include Teflon 2.1, polyethylene 2.25, glass 5–10, and water 80.4. Capacitance depends on both geometry and the dielectric, not geometry alone when materials change.

:::example Complete the primary capacitor geometry calculations
**Source:** Primary p. 14. Use $\varepsilon_{0} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\,\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{m}}$.

**First problem: $1.0\,\mathrm{F}$ with a $1.0\,\mathrm{mm}$ vacuum gap.**

1. Convert $d = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$.
2. Rearrange $C = \frac{\varepsilon_{0} A}{d}$ to $A = \frac{Cd}{\varepsilon_{0}}$.
3. Calculate $A = \frac{\left( 1.0 \right) \left( 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \right)}{\left( 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \right)} = 1.12994 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$.

**Second problem: $A = 2.0\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$, $d = 5.0\,\mathrm{mm}$, and $V = 10{,}000\,\mathrm{V}$.**

1. Convert $d = 0.0050\,\mathrm{m}$.
2. Calculate $C = \frac{\varepsilon_{0} A}{d} = 3.54 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{F} = 3.54\,\mathrm{nF} = 0.00354\,\mathrm{\mu F}$.
3. Calculate $Q = CV = 3.54 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{C} = 35.4\,\mathrm{\mu C}$ on either plate in magnitude.
4. Calculate $E = \frac{V}{d} = 2.0 \times 10^{6}\,\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{m}}$.
5. Check the field independently: $E = \frac{Q}{\left( \varepsilon_{0} A \right)}$ gives the same result.

**Check.** The plate pair's algebraic net charge is zero. $C = \frac{Q}{V}$ uses one plate's charge magnitude, not that zero total.
:::

:::example The omitted companion dielectric calculation
**Source:** Companion p. 4. **Given:** $A = 0.020\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$, $d = 2.0\,\mathrm{mm}$, $\kappa = 4.0$. Approximate the initial air-filled gap as vacuum.

1. Convert $d = 0.0020\,\mathrm{m}$.
2. Calculate $C_{0} = \frac{\varepsilon_{0} A}{d} = 8.85 \times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{F} = 88.5\,\mathrm{pF}$.
3. Multiply by the dielectric constant: $C = \kappa C_{0} = 4.0 \left( 88.5 \right) = 354\,\mathrm{pF}$.

**Source correction.** The printed $353\,\mathrm{pF}$ does not follow from $88.5\,\mathrm{pF}$ and $\kappa = 4.0$. These stated classroom inputs give $354\,\mathrm{pF}$. The presence of a battery does not change the geometric capacitance calculation; it changes which charge or voltage stays fixed.
:::

:::derivation Plate separation changes: connected and isolated cases
These are labeled consequences of the source's parallel-plate law. Keep plate area and dielectric fixed. Change the gap from d to sd, with $s > 0$.

| Quantity | Ideal battery connected | Isolated plates, no leakage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\frac{C_{\mathrm{new}}}{C_{\mathrm{initial}}}$ | $\frac{1}{s}$ | $\frac{1}{s}$ |
| $\frac{V_{\mathrm{new}}}{V_{\mathrm{initial}}}$ | 1 | s |
| $\frac{Q_{\mathrm{new}}}{Q_{\mathrm{initial}}}$ | $\frac{1}{s}$ | 1 |
| $\frac{E_{\mathrm{new}}}{E_{\mathrm{initial}}}$ | $\frac{1}{s}$ | 1 |
| $\frac{U_{\mathrm{new}}}{U_{\mathrm{initial}}}$ | $\frac{1}{s}$ | s |

Derive each row from $C \propto \frac{1}{d}$, $Q = CV$, $E = \frac{V}{d}$, and $U = \frac{Q^{2}}{\left( 2\,\mathrm{C} \right)}$ or $\frac{CV^{2}}{2}$. Moving isolated charged plates apart increases field energy because external mechanical work enters the system. Do not use the dielectric-insertion ratios for a plate-gap change.
:::

Restore every capacitor in the source networks

:::example Two capacitors in series or parallel: full branch values
**Sources:** Primary p. 24; companion p. 6. **Given:** $6.0\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ and $3.0\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ across $18.0\,\mathrm{V}$.

**Series solution.**

1. Calculate $C_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{\left( 6 \times 3 \right)}{\left( 6 + 3 \right)} = 2.0\,\mathrm{\mu F}$.
2. Calculate the common series charge $Q = C_{\mathrm{eq}}V = 2.0 \left( 18.0 \right) = 36.0\,\mathrm{\mu C}$.
3. Find $V_{6} = \frac{Q}{C_{6}} = \frac{36}{6} = 6\,\mathrm{V}$ and $V_{3} = \frac{36}{3} = 12\,\mathrm{V}$.
4. Check $V_{6} + V_{3} = 18\,\mathrm{V}$.

**Parallel solution.**

1. Calculate $C_{\mathrm{eq}} = 6 + 3 = 9.0\,\mathrm{\mu F}$.
2. Set both branch voltages to $18.0\,\mathrm{V}$.
3. Calculate $Q_{6} = 6 \left( 18 \right) = 108\,\mathrm{\mu C}$ and $Q_{3} = 3 \left( 18 \right) = 54\,\mathrm{\mu C}$.
4. Check $Q_{\mathrm{total}} = 162\,\mathrm{\mu C} = C_{\mathrm{eq}}V$.

For the other primary problem, $5.0\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ and $12.0\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ in parallel across $9.0\,\mathrm{V}$ give $C_{\mathrm{eq}} = 17.0\,\mathrm{\mu F}$. Each has $9.0\,\mathrm{V}$. Their charges are $45\,\mathrm{\mu C}$ and $108\,\mathrm{\mu C}$, totaling $153\,\mathrm{\mu C}$.
:::

{{figure:m6-main:25|The original five-capacitor network. The 9 μF element is in series with the entire upper group.}}

:::example Five-capacitor network at $28\,\mathrm{V}$: every branch solved
**Sources:** Primary p. 25; companion p. 6. The upper group has $3\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ and $11\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ branches beside a series pair of $12\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ and $6\,\mathrm{\mu F}$. This group connects in series with $9\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ between a and b.

1. Reduce the right series pair: $C_{\mathrm{right}} = \frac{\left( 12 \times 6 \right)}{\left( 12 + 6 \right)} = 4\,\mathrm{\mu F}$.
2. Add the three parallel branches: $C_{\mathrm{upper}} = 3 + 11 + 4 = 18\,\mathrm{\mu F}$.
3. Combine $18\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ in series with $9\,\mathrm{\mu F}$: $C_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{\left( 18 \times 9 \right)}{\left( 18 + 9 \right)} = 6\,\mathrm{\mu F}$.
4. Apply $28\,\mathrm{V}$: $Q_{\mathrm{series}} = C_{\mathrm{eq}}V_{ab} = 6 \left( 28 \right) = 168\,\mathrm{\mu C}$.
5. Recover group voltages: $V_{\mathrm{upper}} = \frac{168}{18} = \frac{28}{3} V$; $V_{9} = \frac{168}{9} = \frac{56}{3} V$.
6. Use the shared upper voltage for each upper parallel branch.
7. Use the shared right-branch charge for its $12\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ and $6\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ capacitors.

| Capacitor | Voltage magnitude, V | Charge magnitude, $\mathrm{\mu C}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $3\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ | $\frac{28}{3} \approx 9.3333$ | 28 |
| $11\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ | $\frac{28}{3} \approx 9.3333$ | $\frac{308}{3} \approx 102.6667$ |
| $12\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ | $\frac{28}{9} \approx 3.1111$ | $\frac{112}{3} \approx 37.3333$ |
| $6\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ | $\frac{56}{9} \approx 6.2222$ | $\frac{112}{3} \approx 37.3333$ |
| $9\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ | $\frac{56}{3} \approx 18.6667$ | 168 |

**Three checks.** The right-pair voltages sum to $\frac{28}{3} V$. The upper branch charges sum to $168\,\mathrm{\mu C}$. The upper-group and $9\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ voltages sum to $28\,\mathrm{V}$. The full network stores $U = \tfrac{1}{2} C_{\mathrm{eq}}V^{2} = 2352\,\mathrm{\mu J}$.

**Common error.** The $12\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ and $6\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ elements each carry the right branch's charge, not the full network's $168\,\mathrm{\mu C}$.

**Source:** Primary p. 16.

1. Convert $C = 5.80\,\mathrm{\mu F}$ to $5.80 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F}$ and use $V = 400\,\mathrm{V}$.
2. Calculate $U = \tfrac{1}{2} CV^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \left( 5.80 \times 10^{-6} \right) \left( 400^{2} \right) = 0.464\,\mathrm{J}$.
3. For the separate $5.0\,\mathrm{\mu F}$, $1.5\,\mathrm{V}$ problem, use $Q = CV = 7.5\,\mathrm{\mu C}$.

**Check.** Squaring the voltage squares its factor of ten. The first problem's plate separation is not needed once C and V are already supplied.
:::

:::derivation Battery work and stored energy during dielectric insertion
This is a labeled extension. Initially $C_{0}$ and $V_{0}$ describe the capacitor. Insert a dielectric of constant $\kappa$ quasistatically into the entire fixed gap, while an ideal battery stays connected.

1. Find $\Delta Q = \left( \kappa - 1 \right) C_{0} V_{0}$ from $Q = CV$.
2. Calculate battery energy supplied: $W_{\mathrm{battery}} = V_{0} \Delta Q = \left( \kappa - 1 \right) C_{0} V_{0}^{2}$.
3. Calculate the increase in stored field energy: $\Delta U = \tfrac{1}{2} \left( \kappa - 1 \right) C_{0} V_{0}^{2}$.
4. Under the ideal loss-free quasistatic model, the remaining half leaves as mechanical work by the field on the dielectric.

$$W_{field,mech}=W_{battery}-\Delta U
=\frac12(\kappa-1)C_0V_0^2.$$

For an isolated capacitor, the battery supplies no energy. Its field energy decreases from $\frac{Q_{0}^{2}}{\left( 2 C_{0} \right)}$ to $\frac{Q_{0}^{2}}{\left( 2 \kappa C_{0} \right)}$. The decrease can become mechanical work. State the electrical connection before applying energy conservation.
:::

**Applications — primary p. 26.** A camera flash stores energy over a longer charging interval and releases it over a shorter interval. The same energy released in less time gives greater average power, $P_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{\Delta U}{\Delta t}$. Capacitors also smooth changing supply voltages and provide brief charge pulses. Their circuit role depends on the connection, not merely the presence of a capacitor symbol.

Situational problems: choose the law, then solve These added practice problems apply the module concepts. They are not copied examination questions. Keep the stated assumptions when you use each result. #### Situation 1: Dielectric with the battery removed An ideal charged capacitor is disconnected from its battery. A dielectric completely fills its unchanged gap, increasing capacitance by a factor κ>1. Ignore leakage. Which comparison is correct? 1. **Identify the boundary condition.** Disconnection and negligible leakage hold the free plate charge fixed. 2. **Use the new capacitance.** $$C'=\kappa C$$ 3. **Derive voltage and energy ratios.** $$V'=\frac Q{\kappa C}=\frac V\kappa,\quad U'=\frac{Q^2}{2\kappa C}=\frac U\kappa$$ 4. **Account for energy.** Field energy can decrease while the electric force does mechanical work on the inserted material. **Answer:** $Q$ stays fixed, while $V$ and stored field energy each divide by $\kappa$. **Why the other answers do not work:** - **$V$ stays fixed and charge multiplies by $\kappa$.** — That describes a connected ideal voltage source, not this isolated capacitor. - **Charge and energy both stay fixed.** — Charge conservation does not imply fixed field energy. - **Energy multiplies by $\kappa$ because capacitance increases.** — That uses a fixed-voltage energy comparison despite the disconnected battery. #### Situation 2: Why connected insertion needs the source A dielectric is inserted quasistatically while an ideal battery stays connected to a capacitor at fixed voltage. Capacitance increases. How can the capacitor’s stored energy increase while the dielectric is pulled inward? 1. **Use the fixed-voltage condition.** $$Q=CV,\qquad U=\tfrac12CV^2$$ 2. **Compare source work for a change in capacitance.** $$W_{\mathrm{battery}}=V\Delta Q=V^2\Delta C$$ 3. **Compare the stored-energy increase.** $$\Delta U=\tfrac12V^2\Delta C$$ 4. **Identify the remaining energy transfer.** In the ideal quasistatic model, the remaining half can appear as mechanical work. A field-only comparison omits this source contribution. **Answer:** The battery supplies energy; the capacitor field is not an isolated energy system. **Why the other answers do not work:** - **Energy conservation fails for dielectrics.** — Include the source and mechanical work before testing conservation. - **The plate charge must stay fixed because the geometry is fixed.** — A connected battery can transfer charge as capacitance changes. - **A rise in capacitor energy proves the force pushes the dielectric outward.** — That inference omits the battery energy exchange. #### Situation 3: Parallel capacitors after disconnection A charged capacitor is disconnected from its source, then connected in parallel with an initially uncharged equal capacitor, with corresponding plates joined. A small connection resistance allows equilibrium. Which statement is correct? 1. **Conserve charge on the joined positive node.** $$CV_0=(C+C)V_f$$ 2. **Find the shared final voltage.** $$V_f=V_0/2$$ 3. **Compare field energies.** $$U_i=\tfrac12CV_0^2,\quad U_f=\tfrac12(2C)(V_0/2)^2=U_i/2$$ 4. **Complete the energy account.** The finite connection dissipates energy during the transient. Conserving charge does not require conserving field energy alone. **Answer:** Charge is conserved, the final voltage halves, and some initial field energy is dissipated. **Why the other answers do not work:** - **Both charge and capacitor field energy remain entirely in the final electric field.** — The final shared voltage gives a lower total field energy. - **The final voltage remains equal to the original voltage.** — No connected battery holds it there. - **The initially uncharged capacitor cannot acquire charge.** — The joined conductors allow redistribution. #### Situation 4: Series charge and component voltage Two initially uncharged capacitors are placed in series across a battery with an initially neutral isolated intermediate node. One capacitor has three times the other’s capacitance. Which comparison is correct? 1. **Use the intermediate-node condition.** Opposite induced charges on the two inner plates have equal magnitudes. 2. **Apply the component relation.** $$V_1=Q/C_1,\qquad V_2=Q/C_2$$ 3. **Take the ratio.** $$\frac{V_{\mathrm{small}}}{V_{\mathrm{large}}}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{large}}}{C_{\mathrm{small}}}=3$$ 4. **Distinguish parallel.** Parallel connections fix common voltage instead of common series charge. **Answer:** They have equal charge magnitudes; the smaller capacitor has three times the voltage. **Why the other answers do not work:** - **They have equal voltages; the larger has three times the charge.** — That is the parallel condition. - **The larger capacitor must have the larger voltage.** — Voltage is inversely proportional to capacitance at the common series charge. - **Their equivalent capacitance exceeds the larger component.** — A positive series equivalent is smaller than the smallest component. #### Situation 5: Separating isolated capacitor plates An ideal parallel-plate capacitor is charged and isolated. Its plate gap doubles while overlap area and permittivity remain fixed. Ignore fringing and leakage. Which result follows? 1. **Change the geometry.** $$C=\epsilon A/d\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C'=C/2$$ 2. **Hold charge fixed.** $$V'=Q/C'=2V$$ 3. **Use the fixed-charge energy form.** $$U'=Q^2/(2C')=2U$$ 4. **Check the energy transfer.** The external agent’s positive separation work increases stored field energy. **Answer:** Capacitance halves, voltage doubles, and field energy doubles. **Why the other answers do not work:** - **Capacitance doubles because the gap increases.** — Capacitance is inversely proportional to the gap. - **Voltage stays fixed because it was once connected to a battery.** — A removed battery no longer enforces voltage. - **Energy halves because capacitance halves.** — That energy scaling would require fixed voltage, not fixed charge. #### Situation 6: Recovering a series component’s energy Initially uncharged capacitors 3.0 μF and 6.0 μF are in series across 12 V, with a neutral isolated middle node. Find the energy stored in the 3.0 μF capacitor. 1. **Reduce the series pair.** $$C_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{3(6)}{3+6}=2\,\mu\mathrm F$$ 2. **Find common charge.** $$Q=C_{\mathrm{eq}}V=2(12)=24\,\mu\mathrm C$$ 3. **Recover the small capacitor’s voltage.** $$V_3=Q/C_3=24/3=8\,\mathrm V$$ 4. **Calculate that component’s energy.** The 6 μF component has the remaining 4 V, so the recovered voltages add to 12 V. $$U_3=\tfrac12(3.0\times10^{-6})(8)^2$$ 5. **State the result.** $$9.6\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J$$ **Answer:** $9.6\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J$ **Why the other answers do not work:** - **$2.16\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J$** — This incorrectly puts the full 12 V across the 3 μF component. - **$4.8\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J$** — The component energy includes one half, but its actual voltage must first be found. - **$1.44\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J$** — This is the total energy of the series combination. #### Situation 7: Isolated dielectric insertion A 2.0 μF capacitor is charged to 10 V and disconnected. An ideal dielectric of $\kappa=3$ fully fills the unchanged gap without leakage. Find the final stored energy. 1. **Find the charge before disconnection.** $$Q=(2.0\times10^{-6})(10)=20\,\mu\mathrm C$$ 2. **Apply the dielectric change.** $$C'=3C=6.0\,\mu\mathrm F$$ 3. **Hold charge fixed.** $$U'=\frac{Q^2}{2C'}=\frac{(20\times10^{-6})^2}{2(6.0\times10^{-6})}$$ 4. **Check the comparison.** The initial energy is 100 μJ. Dividing by $\kappa=3$ gives the final field energy. 5. **State the result.** $$3.33333\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J$$ **Answer:** $3.33333\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J$ **Why the other answers do not work:** - **$3\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J$** — This uses the connected fixed-voltage scaling. - **$1\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J$** — This assumes unchanged field energy despite the mechanical interaction. - **$1.11111\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J$** — This divides the energy by κ² rather than κ at fixed charge. #### Situation 8: Battery work during dielectric insertion An ideal battery keeps 12 V across an initially 2.0 μF capacitor. A dielectric increases its capacitance to 8.0 μF during quasistatic insertion. Find the energy supplied by the battery, not just the capacitor-energy change. 1. **Find the capacitance increase.** $$\Delta C=(8.0-2.0)\,\mu\mathrm F=6.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$$ 2. **Find charge delivered at fixed voltage.** $$\Delta Q=V\Delta C=12(6.0\times10^{-6})=72\,\mu\mathrm C$$ 3. **Calculate source work.** $$W_{\mathrm{battery}}=V\Delta Q=12(72\times10^{-6})$$ 4. **Check the larger energy account.** The rest can become mechanical work in the stated quasistatic idealization. $$\Delta U=\tfrac12\Delta CV^2=432\,\mu\mathrm J$$ 5. **State the result.** $$8.64\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J$$ **Answer:** $8.64\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J$ **Why the other answers do not work:** - **$4.32\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J$** — This is the capacitor’s stored-energy increase, half the ideal battery work for this process. - **$0.001152\,\mathrm J$** — This counts the full final CV² rather than the change in delivered charge. - **$2.88\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J$** — This omits the actual capacitance change. #### Situation 9: Geometry change after isolation An ideal parallel-plate capacitor has area 0.030 m², gap 1.2 mm, and dielectric constant $\kappa=2$. It is charged to 100 V and isolated. The gap then doubles while the dielectric still completely fills it and κ remains fixed. Find the final stored energy. Use $\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$. 1. **Convert the original gap.** $$d_0=1.2\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm m$$ 2. **Find the initial capacitance.** $$C_0=\frac{\kappa\epsilon_0A}{d_0}=4.425\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm F$$ 3. **Hold the isolated charge fixed as the gap doubles.** $$C_f=C_0/2,\qquad Q=C_0V_0$$ 4. **Use the final capacitance with that fixed charge.** The final energy is twice the initial energy. External work separates the attracting plates. $$U_f=\frac{(C_0V_0)^2}{2(C_0/2)}=C_0V_0^2$$ 5. **State the result.** $$4.425\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm J$$ **Answer:** $4.425\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm J$ **Why the other answers do not work:** - **$1.10625\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm J$** — This applies fixed-voltage scaling to an isolated capacitor. - **$2.2125\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm J$** — This is the initial field energy. - **$8.85\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm J$** — This doubles the correct final energy again. #### Situation 10: Unequally charged capacitors share charge Isolated capacitors 2.0 μF at 10 V and 3.0 μF at 4 V are connected in parallel with corresponding positive plates joined. A small resistance allows equilibrium. Find the final common voltage. 1. **Find charge on the joined positive node.** $$Q_{\mathrm{total}}=(2)(10)+(3)(4)=32\,\mu\mathrm C$$ 2. **Find the final parallel capacitance.** $$C_f=2+3=5\,\mu\mathrm F$$ 3. **Divide conserved charge by final capacitance.** $$V_f=32/5=6.4\,\mathrm V$$ 4. **Check the energy difference.** The transient dissipates 21.6 μJ; conserving charge alone does not keep all initial energy in the final electric field. $$U_i=124\,\mu\mathrm J,\quad U_f=102.4\,\mu\mathrm J$$ 5. **State the result.** $$6.4\,\mathrm V$$ **Answer:** $6.4\,\mathrm V$ **Why the other answers do not work:** - **$7\,\mathrm V$** — This averages voltages without capacitance weighting. - **$8\,\mathrm V$** — Conserve the joined-node charge rather than selecting an arbitrary intermediate voltage. - **$14\,\mathrm V$** — Parallel connection does not add the original voltages.

Situation 11: A series capacitor feeds a parallel pair · Find the equivalent capacitance

An initially uncharged capacitor $C_1=3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$ connects in series with a parallel pair $C_2=2.0\,\mu\mathrm F$ and $C_3=4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$. An ideal 12 V source connects across the complete network. The internal connecting node starts neutral. Use the final steady electrostatic state. Find the equivalent capacitance. 1. **Identify the model and the conditions.** Combine the parallel pair first. The series branch charges have equal magnitudes; the parallel capacitors share voltage. 2. **Reduce the parallel pair.** $$C_p=C_2+C_3=6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$$ 3. **Reduce the remaining series pair.** $$C_{\rm eq}=C_1C_p/(C_1+C_p)=2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$$ 4. **Recover branch charge and voltage.** $$Q_1=C_{\rm eq}V=2.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C,\quad V_p=Q_1/C_p=4\,\mathrm V$$ 5. **Solve the requested quantity.** $$C_{\rm eq}=\frac{3\times10^{-6}(6\times10^{-6})}{9\times10^{-6}}$$ 6. **Check the physical result.** The total series capacitance is below either of its two branch capacitances. 7. **State the result.** $$2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$$ **Answer:** $2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$ **Why the other answers do not work:** - **$9\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$** — This treats the whole network as parallel. - **$9.23077\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm F$** — This treats the parallel pair as series. - **$6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$** — This omits the series capacitor.

Situation 12: A series capacitor feeds a parallel pair · Find the magnitude of charge on C1

An initially uncharged capacitor $C_1=3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$ connects in series with a parallel pair $C_2=2.0\,\mu\mathrm F$ and $C_3=4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$. An ideal 12 V source connects across the complete network. The internal connecting node starts neutral. Use the final steady electrostatic state. Find the magnitude of charge on C1. 1. **Identify the model and the conditions.** Combine the parallel pair first. The series branch charges have equal magnitudes; the parallel capacitors share voltage. 2. **Reduce the parallel pair.** $$C_p=C_2+C_3=6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$$ 3. **Reduce the remaining series pair.** $$C_{\rm eq}=C_1C_p/(C_1+C_p)=2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$$ 4. **Recover branch charge and voltage.** $$Q_1=C_{\rm eq}V=2.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C,\quad V_p=Q_1/C_p=4\,\mathrm V$$ 5. **Solve the requested quantity.** $$Q_1=C_{\rm eq}V=2\times10^{-6}(12)$$ 6. **Check the physical result.** Equal series charge applies to C1 and the whole parallel branch, not separately to C2 and C3. 7. **State the result.** $$2.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C$$ **Answer:** $2.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C$ **Why the other answers do not work:** - **$3.6\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C$** — C1 does not receive the full source voltage. - **$7.2\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C$** — The parallel pair does not receive the full source voltage. - **$1.2\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C$** — Series branch charge magnitudes are equal; source voltage is not split by halving the charge.

Situation 13: A series capacitor feeds a parallel pair · Find the voltage across C3

An initially uncharged capacitor $C_1=3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$ connects in series with a parallel pair $C_2=2.0\,\mu\mathrm F$ and $C_3=4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$. An ideal 12 V source connects across the complete network. The internal connecting node starts neutral. Use the final steady electrostatic state. Find the voltage across C3. 1. **Identify the model and the conditions.** Combine the parallel pair first. The series branch charges have equal magnitudes; the parallel capacitors share voltage. 2. **Reduce the parallel pair.** $$C_p=C_2+C_3=6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$$ 3. **Reduce the remaining series pair.** $$C_{\rm eq}=C_1C_p/(C_1+C_p)=2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$$ 4. **Recover branch charge and voltage.** $$Q_1=C_{\rm eq}V=2.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C,\quad V_p=Q_1/C_p=4\,\mathrm V$$ 5. **Solve the requested quantity.** $$V_3=V_p=Q_1/(C_2+C_3)=4\,\mathrm V$$ 6. **Check the physical result.** C2 and C3 share the same parallel voltage. 7. **State the result.** $$4\,\mathrm V$$ **Answer:** $4\,\mathrm V$ **Why the other answers do not work:** - **$12\,\mathrm V$** — The series capacitor takes part of the total voltage. - **$8\,\mathrm V$** — This gives the voltage across C1. - **$6\,\mathrm V$** — The whole branch charge is shared by C2 and C3.

Situation 14: A series capacitor feeds a parallel pair · Find the energy stored in C3 alone

An initially uncharged capacitor $C_1=3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$ connects in series with a parallel pair $C_2=2.0\,\mu\mathrm F$ and $C_3=4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$. An ideal 12 V source connects across the complete network. The internal connecting node starts neutral. Use the final steady electrostatic state. Find the energy stored in C3 alone. 1. **Identify the model and the conditions.** Combine the parallel pair first. An initially uncharged capacitor $C_1=3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$ connects in series with a parallel pair $C_2=2.0\,\mu\mathrm F$ and $C_3=4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F$. Situation 21: A dielectric covers only part of the area · Find the final capacitance

title: Current & DC circuits
headline: Current and DC circuits: label nodes, currents, and polarity
summary: Current, material properties, DC networks, Kirchhoff rules, and RC transients.

sections.title: Derive drift current and macroscopic resistance
sections.search:
## Current and DC circuits: label nodes, currents, and polarity

Current is signed charge flow per time: $I = \frac{dQ}{dt}$, or $\frac{Q}{\Delta t}$ for a constant average flow. One ampere is one $\frac{C}{s}$. Conventional current points as positive charge would move. Electron drift in a metal points the opposite way. Random microscopic motion alone gives no net current. Current through a branch is a signed scalar; current density J is a vector.

Derive drift current and macroscopic resistance

In time $\Delta t$, carriers drift through volume $Av_{d} \Delta t$. With number density n and charge magnitude |q|, charge crossing the area is $nAv_{d} \Delta t \left| q \right|$. Divide by $\Delta t$:

$$I=n|q|Av_d,\quad J=I/A=n|q|v_d,\quad \mathbf J=nq\mathbf v_d.$$

The vector expression keeps the signed charge. Carrier concentration has units $m^{-3}$, not $\frac{C}{m^{3}}$. Current from several carrier populations adds. J parallel to E is the simple isotropic ohmic model; it is not a universal statement for every medium and magnetic-field condition.

**Worked examples — primary pp. 16–17.** $29.3\,\mathrm{C}$ in $7.84\,\mathrm{s}$ gives $3.737\,\mathrm{A}$. A $0.010\,\mathrm{A}$ calculator for $60\,\mathrm{s}$ transfers $0.600\,\mathrm{C}$. $J = 50\,\frac{\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{m}^{2}}$, $q = - 0.10\,\mathrm{C}$, and $v_{d} = - 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$ give $n = \frac{J}{\left( qv_{d} \right)} = 2.5 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$. The unusually large individual charge is the source's hypothetical value, not an electron charge.

For an ohmic isotropic material, $E = \rho J$ and conductivity $\sigma = \frac{1}{\rho}$. Substitute $E = \frac{V}{L}$ and $J = \frac{I}{A}$ for a uniform wire:

$$\frac VL=\rho\frac IA\Rightarrow V=IR,\quad R=\frac{\rho L}{A},\quad \rho=\frac{RA}{L}.$$

Resistivity $\rho$ has units Ω·m; resistance R has units Ω. For a circular wire $A = \pi r^{2} = \frac{\pi d^{2}}{4}$. Doubling LENGTH at fixed area doubles R. Doubling DIAMETER at fixed length divides R by four. For the same wire stretched without volume change, $A = \frac{V_{\mathrm{wire}}}{L}$, so $R = \frac{\rho L^{2}}{V_{\mathrm{wire}}}$ if resistivity stays constant.

sections.title: Temperature, ohmic behavior, and resistor identification
sections.search:
Temperature, ohmic behavior, and resistor identification

Near a reference temperature, $R = R_{0} \left[ 1 + \alpha \left( T - T_{0} \right) \right]$, and similarly for resistivity. Rearrange $\alpha = \frac{\left( \frac{R}{R_{0}} - 1 \right)}{\left( T - T_{0} \right)}$. This linear approximation can fail over a large temperature range. Do not confuse the resistance-temperature coefficient with thermal-expansion $\alpha$. $R_{0}$ is resistance when used in the R equation, despite the source's occasional “resistivity” label.

Ohm's law means a linear V–I relation under stable material conditions. A lamp heating up need not have a constant resistance. Carbon/semiconductor temperature behavior can differ from metals.

The source includes resistor color bands. For a four-band resistor, the first two colors give digits, the third gives a power-of-ten multiplier, and the fourth gives tolerance. Digit sequence: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. Gold/silver commonly represent multipliers $\frac{10^{-1}}{10^{-2}}$ or tolerances ±5%/±10%. Read the band roles and orientation, not only the colors.

sections.title: Electrical power, energy, and internal resistance
sections.search:
Electrical power, energy, and internal resistance

An amount dq crossing voltage V transfers energy $dW = Vdq$. Divide by dt:

$$P=VI,\quad P_R=I^2R=V_R^2/R,\quad E_{energy}=Pt.$$

The resistor substitutions require Ohm's law. A kilowatt-hour is an ENERGY unit: $1\,\mathrm{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{J}$. It is not “kilowatts per hour.” At fixed V, increasing R lowers resistor power; at fixed I, increasing R raises it.

A real source has emf $\mathcal{E}$ and internal resistance r. For discharging current I, terminal voltage $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ and $I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{\left( R + r \right)}$. During charging with current driven into the positive terminal, $V = \mathcal{E} + Ir$ under that stated convention. Emf is energy supplied per charge, not a mechanical force.

**Worked example — companion heating element.** $R = 20 \Omega$ on $120\,\mathrm{V}$ gives $I = 6\,\mathrm{A}$ and $P = 720\,\mathrm{W}$. In $15\,\mathrm{min} = 900\,\mathrm{s}$, energy: $648{,}000\,\mathrm{J} = 0.18\,\mathrm{kWh}$. Increasing R to $30\,\Omega$ at the same voltage gives $480\,\mathrm{W}$, not greater power.

sections.title: Derive series and parallel resistor rules
sections.search:
Derive series and parallel resistor rules

Series resistors have a common current if there is no branch at their connecting node. $V_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum IR_{i}$ gives $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum R_{i}$. Therefore $\frac{V_{i}}{V_{\mathrm{tot}}} = \frac{R_{i}}{R_{\mathrm{eq}}}$: the voltage-divider relation.

Parallel resistors share the same two nodes and voltage. $I_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_i\frac{V}{R_i}$ gives $\frac1{R_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\sum_i\frac1{R_i}$. For two, $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{R_{1} R_{2}}{\left( R_{1} + R_{2} \right)}$. Their current ratio is $\frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}} = \frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}}$. An equivalent parallel resistance must be smaller than the smallest positive branch resistance.

**Worked example.** Put $3\,\Omega$ and $6\,\Omega$ in parallel across $12\,\mathrm{V}$. $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = 2 \Omega$; branch currents are $4\,\mathrm{A}$ and $2\,\mathrm{A}$; total is $6\,\mathrm{A}$. Total power: $12 \times 6 = 72\,\mathrm{W}$, also $4^{2} \times 3 + 2^{2} \times 6 = 72\,\mathrm{W}$. A series $4\,\Omega$ added before that group gives $6\,\Omega$ overall. The source current becomes $2\,\mathrm{A}$, the parallel-group drop becomes $4\,\mathrm{V}$, and its branch currents become $\frac{4}{3} A$ and $\frac{2}{3} A$.

An ideal ammeter goes in SERIES and has zero resistance. An ideal voltmeter goes in PARALLEL and has infinite resistance. An ideal wire shorts points into one node. A shorted resistor has zero voltage, not its previous unmodified branch voltage. Do not reduce an arbitrary bridge as series/parallel when the required node conditions fail.

sections.title: Kirchhoff rules: derive the equations and keep the signs
sections.search:
Kirchhoff rules: derive the equations and keep the signs

KCL follows conservation of charge at a steady node: $\sum I_{\mathrm{in}} = \sum I_{\mathrm{out}}$. KVL follows energy balance around a lumped DC loop: $\sum \Delta V = 0$. A resistor traversed with the chosen current gives −IR; traversed against it gives +IR. Across an ideal battery, negative-to-positive gives $+ \mathcal{E}$ and the reverse gives $- \mathcal{E}$.

Choose arbitrary current directions, write independent equations, and solve them simultaneously. A negative answer reverses the assumed direction; it is not a negative physical resistance. Do not change an assumed arrow midway through the algebra.

**Worked example — companion p. 14 type.** A loop has a $12\,\mathrm{V}$ aiding source, an opposing $6\,\mathrm{V}$ source, and 6 Ω total resistance. KVL gives $12 - 6 - 6 I = 0$, so $I = 1\,\mathrm{A}$. If both sources aided, the same resistance would give $3\,\mathrm{A}$.

**Primary multi-branch example, pp. 70–74.** Preserve the source's chosen arrows. Its independent equations are $I_{3} = I_{1} + I_{2}$, $30 I_{1} + 41 I_{3} = 45$, and $- 30 I_{1} + 21 I_{2} = 80$. Solving without early rounding gives $I_{1} = - \frac{2335}{2721} \approx - 0.85814\,\mathrm{A}$, $I_{2} \approx 2.58361\,\mathrm{A}$, and $I_{3} \approx 1.72547\,\mathrm{A}$. Substitute all three into the ORIGINAL equations. The negative $I_{1}$ reverses its chosen arrow. The printed intermediate rounded expressions obscure this small difference.

**Show the elimination.** Substitute $I_{3} = I_{1} + I_{2}$ into the first loop. This produces $71 I_{1} + 41 I_{2} = 45$. Keep $- 30 I_{1} + 21 I_{2} = 80$ as the second loop. Multiply the first equation by 30 and the second by 71. Add them to remove $I_{1}$:

$$\begin{aligned}2130I_1+1230I_2&=1350,\\-2130I_1+1491I_2&=5680,\\2721I_2&=7030.\end{aligned}$$

Thus $I_{2} = \frac{7030}{2721}$. Back-substitution gives $I_{1} = \frac{\left( 21 I_{2} - 80 \right)}{30} = - \frac{2335}{2721}$ and $I_{3} = \frac{4695}{2721}$. Check KCL: $- 0.858140 + 2.583609 = 1.725469\,\mathrm{A}$. Check the loops with full precision: $30 I_{1} + 41 I_{3} = 45\,\mathrm{V}$ and $- 30 I_{1} + 21 I_{2} = 80\,\mathrm{V}$. A small residual after using rounded displayed currents is a rounding effect; a large residual needs corrected signs or algebra.

sections.title: RC charging and discharging: derive the exponentials
sections.search:
RC charging and discharging: derive the exponentials

For an initially uncharged capacitor C charged through R from constant emf $\mathcal{E}$, KVL gives $\mathcal{E} - R \left( \frac{dq}{dt} \right) - \frac{q}{C} = 0$. Separate $\frac{dq}{\left( C\mathcal{E} - q \right)} = \frac{dt}{\left( RC \right)}$. Integrate with $q \left( 0 \right) = 0$:

$$q=C\mathcal E(1-e^{-t/RC}),\quad V_C=\mathcal E(1-e^{-t/RC}),\quad I=\frac{\mathcal E}{R}e^{-t/RC}.$$

For discharging through R, $R \left( \frac{dq}{dt} \right) + \frac{q}{C} = 0$, so $q = Q_{0} \exp \left( - \frac{t}{\left( RC \right)} \right)$ and $V_{C} = V_{0} \exp \left( - \frac{t}{\left( RC \right)} \right)$. The signed current depends on its reference arrow; its magnitude is $\frac{V_{0} \exp \left( - \frac{t}{\left( RC \right)} \right)}{R}$. The capacitor voltage cannot jump instantaneously in this ideal finite-current model.

$$\tau_{RC}=RC,\quad t_{discharge}=-RC\ln f,\quad t_{charge}=-RC\ln(1-f).$$

At one $\tau$, discharge leaves 36.8%; charging reaches 63.2%. “63%” is rounded, so exactly 63.000% is not exactly one $\tau$. For an arbitrary initial voltage $V_{0}$, $V_{C} \left( t \right) = V_{f} + \left( V_{0} - V_{f} \right) \exp \left( - \frac{t}{\left( RC \right)} \right)$. A network's relevant R is the resistance seen by the capacitor with independent ideal sources appropriately deactivated, not always the sum of all printed resistors.

**Worked example — primary p. 79.** $C = 35\,\mathrm{\mu F}$, $R = 120 \Omega$. $\tau = 0.00420\,\mathrm{s}$. To reach 10% of the initial voltage, $t = - 0.00420 \ln \left( 0.10 \right) = 0.009671\,\mathrm{s} = 9.67\,\mathrm{ms}$. Do not enter 10 in place of 0.10.

**Show the charging integration.** The separated equation integrates from $q = 0$ to q(t), and from time 0 to t. The minus sign comes from differentiating $C\mathcal{E} - q$:

$$-\ln\left(\frac{C\mathcal E-q}{C\mathcal E}\right)=\frac{t}{RC}\Rightarrow 1-\frac q{C\mathcal E}=e^{-t/RC}.$$

For $R = 2.0 k\Omega$, $C = 10\,\mathrm{\mu F}$, and $\mathcal{E} = 12\,\mathrm{V}$, $\tau = 0.020\,\mathrm{s}$ and $Q_{\mathrm{final}} = 120\,\mathrm{\mu C}$. At $t = 0.020\,\mathrm{s}$, $q \approx 75.854\,\mathrm{\mu C}$, $V_{C} \approx 7.58545\,\mathrm{V}$, and $I \approx 2.20728\,\mathrm{mA}$. Check KVL: $RI + V_{C} = 4.41455 + 7.58545 = 12\,\mathrm{V}$. To reach 90%, solve $t = - 0.020 \ln \left( 0.10 \right) \approx 0.04605\,\mathrm{s}$.

**Transient energy extension.** During a complete ideal RC charge from zero, the battery supplies $\int \mathcal{E} I dt = C\mathcal{E}^{2}$. The capacitor stores $\frac{C\mathcal{E}^{2}}{2}$. The resistor dissipates the remaining $\frac{C\mathcal{E}^{2}}{2}$, independent of positive R in this model. A smaller R changes the time and peak power; it does not remove that total dissipated energy.

sections.title: Finish the current, resistivity, and resistor-identification material
sections.search:
Finish the current, resistivity, and resistor-identification material

**Current carriers.** The primary's “flow of electrons” definition describes a metal, but current more generally means net charge flow. Positive and negative ions can also carry current. A closed circuit provides a continuous conducting path. An open branch carries no steady conduction current in this model. A short circuit provides a low-resistance path; an actual source's internal resistance still limits its current.

**Circuit symbols — primary p. 37.** The longer battery line marks the positive terminal. An A in a circle denotes an ammeter in the measured branch. A V in a circle denotes a voltmeter connected across two nodes. A connection dot identifies joined wires. Label the nodes before deciding whether two components share a voltage.

**Current and the body — primary p. 15.** The source table associates increasing current with sensation, muscle effects, disrupted breathing, and heart effects. Its ranges are illustrative, not universal thresholds. Effects also depend on the current path and contact duration. [OSHA's electrical-safety material](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA3075.pdf) explains these dependencies. The original table remains available in the source reader.

:::derivation Drift, collision time, and microscopic Ohm's law
**Source starting point:** Primary p. 7. The additional algebra uses a simple relaxation-time model.

1. Between collisions, the carrier acceleration is $a = \frac{qE}{m}$.
2. The model's mean drift velocity is $v_{d} = \frac{qE\tau _{\mathrm{collision}}}{m}$.
3. Insert vd into $J = nqv_{d}$.
4. Compare the result with $J = \sigma E$.

$$\mathbf J=\frac{nq^2\tau_{collision}}m\mathbf E,
\qquad \sigma=\frac{nq^2\tau_{collision}}m,
\qquad \rho=\frac{m}{nq^2\tau_{collision}}.$$

The squared charge makes $\sigma$ positive for either carrier sign. For electrons, vd opposes E while J points along E. This is a microscopic model for suitable materials; it is not an exact conductivity theory for every substance.
:::

:::example All three primary current calculations
**Source:** Primary p. 17.

1. For $29.3\,\mathrm{C}$ passing in $7.84\,\mathrm{s}$, $I_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{29.3}{7.84} = 3.73724\,\mathrm{A}$, about $3.74\,\mathrm{A}$.
2. For a constant calculator current of $0.010\,\mathrm{A}$ for $60\,\mathrm{s}$, $Q = I\Delta t = 0.600\,\mathrm{C}$.
3. For $15\,\mathrm{C}$ passing in $3\,\mathrm{s}$, $I_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{15}{3} = 5\,\mathrm{A}$.

**Check.** Coulombs divided by seconds give amperes. These are average values unless the flow is constant. For a varying current, use $Q = \int I \left( t \right) dt$.
:::

:::example Carrier concentration with signed vectors
**Source:** Primary p. 16. **Given:** $J_{x} = + 50.0\,\frac{\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{m}^{2}}$, $q = - 0.10\,\mathrm{C}$, and $v_{dx} = - 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$.

1. Use $J_{x} = nqv_{dx}$, keeping both negative signs.
2. Calculate $qv_{dx} = \left( - 0.10 \right) \left( - 2.0 \times 10^{-4} \right) = + \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{C} \cdot m}{s}$.
3. Divide $n = \frac{50.0}{\left( 2.0 \times 10^{-5} \right)} = 2.5 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

**Check.** A carrier count per volume must be positive. The supplied $- 0.10\,\mathrm{C}$ is a hypothetical carrier charge, not an electron's charge.
:::

{{figure:m7-main:21|The primary resistivity and temperature-coefficient table. Values depend on material composition and the reference temperature.}}

The companion also lists conductors, semiconductors, and insulators. Metals generally have low resistivity. Insulators have much higher resistivity. Semiconductor resistivity strongly depends on temperature and impurities. Its graph shows that superconducting resistivity becomes zero below a material-dependent critical temperature under suitable conditions. Do not extrapolate the room-temperature linear resistance model through that transition.

:::example Copper resistivity at 70°C
**Source:** Companion pp. 3–4. **Given:** $\rho_{0} = 1.68 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \cdot m$ at 20°C; $\alpha = 0.0039^{\circ} C^{-1}$.

1. Find $\Delta T = 70 - 20 = 50^{\circ} C$.
2. Calculate the dimensionless correction: $1 + \alpha \Delta T = 1 + 0.0039 \left( 50 \right) = 1.195$.
3. Calculate $\rho = \rho_{0} \left( 1 + \alpha \Delta T \right) = 2.0076 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \cdot m$.
4. Round to the source's $2.01 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \cdot m$.

**Check.** Copper's positive $\alpha$ predicts increased resistivity when heated. Use the supplied $1.68 \times 10^{-8}$ value rather than substituting a different table value halfway through.
:::

{{figure:m7-main:23|The source shows a six-band resistor. Its band roles differ from a four-band resistor.}}

**Four, five, and six bands.** Four bands use two significant digits, a multiplier, and tolerance. Five bands use three significant digits, a multiplier, and tolerance. Six bands add a temperature coefficient, commonly expressed in parts per million per kelvin. The source's pictured six-band resistor is green–blue–black–red–gold–yellow.

:::example Read the pictured six-band resistor
**Source:** Primary p. 23.

1. Read the first three digits: green 5, blue 6, black 0. The significant number is 560.
2. Apply the red multiplier, $10^{2}$: $R_{\mathrm{nominal}} = 560 \left( 100 \right) = 56{,}000 \Omega = 56 k\Omega$.
3. Apply the gold tolerance, ±5%: $\Delta R = 0.05 \left( 56{,}000 \right) = 2800 \Omega$.
4. Find the tolerance interval: 53.2 kΩ to 58.8 kΩ.
5. Read the yellow temperature coefficient as $\frac{25\,\mathrm{ppm}}{K}$ in the displayed code convention.
6. For a $20\,\mathrm{K}$ change, the fractional temperature shift is $25 \times 10^{-6} \left( 20 \right) = 0.0005$, or 0.05%.

**Check.** Manufacturing tolerance and temperature drift describe different effects. Do not treat the sixth band as another multiplier or another significant digit.
:::

Complete the primary Ohm's-law and power exercises

:::example Three missing Ohm's-law answers
**Sources:** Primary pp. 30–32. Assume the stated resistance remains constant.

| Problem | Equation choice and conversion | Solution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 250 Ω bulb at $110\,\mathrm{V}$ | $I = \frac{V}{R}$ | $I = \frac{110}{250} = 0.440\,\mathrm{A}$ |
| Toaster at $220\,\mathrm{V}$ carrying $0.50\,\mathrm{A}$ | $R = \frac{V}{I}$ | $R = \frac{220}{0.50} = 440 \Omega$ |
| 1200 Ω resistor carrying $30\,\mathrm{mA}$ | $I = 0.030\,\mathrm{A}$; $V = IR$ | $V = 0.030 \left( 1200 \right) = 36\,\mathrm{V}$ |

**Check.** Convert milliamperes before using ohms. A physical incandescent bulb changes resistance as it heats; the source exercises use an assigned steady resistance.
:::

:::example Power and energy: choose the form that uses the given values
**Sources:** Primary pp. 39–40; companion pp. 6–7.

1. For $R = 120 \Omega$ and $I = 0.9\,\mathrm{A}$, use $P = I^{2} R = 0.9^{2} \left( 120 \right) = 97.2\,\mathrm{W}$.
2. For $P = 30\,\mathrm{W}$ and $V = 110\,\mathrm{V}$, use $I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{30}{110} = 0.272727\,\mathrm{A}$.
3. For the companion heater, use $R = 20 \Omega$ and $V = 120\,\mathrm{V}$: $I = 6\,\mathrm{A}$ and $P = VI = 720\,\mathrm{W}$.
4. Convert 15 minutes to $900\,\mathrm{s}$, then calculate $E_{\mathrm{energy}} = Pt = 720 \left( 900 \right) = 648{,}000\,\mathrm{J}$.
5. Convert independently: $0.720\,\mathrm{kW} \times 0.25 h = 0.18\,\mathrm{kWh}$.
6. Raise the heater resistance to 30 Ω at fixed $120\,\mathrm{V}$. The new power is $\frac{V^{2}}{R} = 480\,\mathrm{W}$.

**Source correction.** Primary p. 40 labels its $30\,\mathrm{W}$ given value as R. Watts measure power, so the symbol must be P. The resistor formulas $P = I^{2} R$ and $\frac{V^{2}}{R}$ require the resistor's voltage and current.
:::

:::example Real battery: current, terminal voltage, and the complete power budget
**Sources:** Primary pp. 43–44; companion p. 6. **Given:** $\mathcal{E} = 12\,\mathrm{V}$, internal resistance $r = 2 \Omega$, and external load $R = 4 \Omega$.

1. Add the series resistances: $R_{\mathrm{total}} = R + r = 6 \Omega$.
2. Calculate $I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{\left( R + r \right)} = \frac{12}{6} = 2\,\mathrm{A}$.
3. Calculate terminal voltage: $V_{\mathrm{terminal}} = \mathcal{E} - Ir = 12 - 2 \left( 2 \right) = 8\,\mathrm{V}$.
4. Check the load voltage: $IR = 2 \left( 4 \right) = 8\,\mathrm{V}$.
5. Calculate chemical-to-electrical conversion rate: $P_{\mathrm{source}} = \mathcal{E} I = 24\,\mathrm{W}$.
6. Calculate internal heating: $P_{\mathrm{internal}} = I^{2} r = 8\,\mathrm{W}$.
7. Calculate useful load power: $P_{\mathrm{load}} = I^{2} R = 16\,\mathrm{W}$.

**Check.** $24\,\mathrm{W} = 8\,\mathrm{W} + 16\,\mathrm{W}$. The ideal voltmeter reads $8\,\mathrm{V}$; the ideal series ammeter reads $2\,\mathrm{A}$.

For charging at a specified current entering the positive terminal, the required terminal voltage is $\mathcal{E} + Ir$. The incoming power splits into chemical storage $\mathcal{E} I$ and internal heating $I^{2} r$.
:::

Recover every series, parallel, and mixed-network result

:::example The primary 18 kΩ circuit, including its unprinted branch results
**Source:** Primary p. 53. **Given:** 3 kΩ, 10 kΩ, and 5 kΩ in series across $9\,\mathrm{V}$.

1. Add the resistances: $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = 18 k\Omega$.
2. Calculate $I = \frac{9}{18{,}000} = 0.000500\,\mathrm{A} = 0.500\,\mathrm{mA}$.
3. Calculate voltage drops: $1.50\,\mathrm{V}$ across 3 kΩ, $5.00\,\mathrm{V}$ across 10 kΩ, and $2.50\,\mathrm{V}$ across 5 kΩ.
4. Check their sum: $1.50 + 5.00 + 2.50 = 9.00\,\mathrm{V}$.

**Check.** Every series resistor carries $0.500\,\mathrm{mA}$. The largest resistance receives the largest voltage drop.
:::

:::example Primary 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 5 Ω network at $50\,\mathrm{V}$
**Sources:** Primary pp. 54–56.

**Series.** $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 \Omega$. The common current is $\frac{50}{10} = 5\,\mathrm{A}$. The voltage drops are $10\,\mathrm{V}$, $15\,\mathrm{V}$, and $25\,\mathrm{V}$. Their sum is $50\,\mathrm{V}$. Total power is $250\,\mathrm{W}$.

**Parallel.** Every branch has $50\,\mathrm{V}$. Calculate each current separately: $I_{2} \Omega = 25\,\mathrm{A}$, $I_{3} \Omega = \frac{50}{3} A$, and $I_{5} \Omega = 10\,\mathrm{A}$. Their sum is $\frac{155}{3} A$, about $51.6667\,\mathrm{A}$.

$$\frac1{R_{eq}}=\frac12+\frac13+\frac15=\frac{31}{30},
\qquad R_{eq}=\frac{30}{31}\ \Omega\approx0.967742\ \Omega.$$

**Check.** The parallel equivalent is smaller than 2 Ω. It draws more total current than the series connection at the same source voltage.
:::

{{figure:m7-dyn:9|The companion series solution includes an incorrect 8 Ω voltage result. The corrected calculation appears below.}}

:::example Companion 15 Ω, 4 Ω, and 8 Ω circuits at $9\,\mathrm{V}$
**Sources:** Companion pp. 8–10.

**Series.** $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = 15 + 4 + 8 = 27 \Omega$. Use the exact current $I = \frac{9}{27} = \frac{1}{3} A$. The drops are $\frac{15}{3} = 5\,\mathrm{V}$, $\frac{4}{3} = 1.3333\,\mathrm{V}$, and $\frac{8}{3} = 2.6667\,\mathrm{V}$. Their sum is $9\,\mathrm{V}$.

**Source correction.** The series slide prints $1.66\,\mathrm{V}$ for the 8 Ω resistor. That value is incorrect. It also repeats a 4 Ω factor in the wrong row. The physical voltage drop across 8 Ω is $2.6667\,\mathrm{V}$ under the stated circuit.

**Parallel.** Each branch has $9\,\mathrm{V}$. The currents are $\frac{9}{15} = 0.600\,\mathrm{A}$, $\frac{9}{4} = 2.250\,\mathrm{A}$, and $\frac{9}{8} = 1.125\,\mathrm{A}$. Their sum is $3.975\,\mathrm{A}$. The reciprocal sum gives $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{120}{53} \Omega \approx 2.26415 \Omega$. Use unrounded values to check $I = \frac{V}{R_{\mathrm{eq}}}$.
:::

:::example Companion mixed resistor network
**Sources:** Companion pp. 10–11. **Given topology:** 90 Ω in parallel with 45 Ω; that group in series with 10 Ω; that branch in parallel with 25 Ω.

1. Reduce the inner parallel group: $R_{23} = \frac{\left( 90 \times 45 \right)}{\left( 90 + 45 \right)} = 30 \Omega$.
2. Add its series resistor: $R_{123} = 10 + 30 = 40 \Omega$.
3. Combine the two outer branches: $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{\left( 40 \times 25 \right)}{\left( 40 + 25 \right)} = \frac{200}{13} \Omega \approx 15.3846 \Omega$.
4. Check that the final equivalent is smaller than either outer parallel branch, 25 Ω and 40 Ω.

**Reason for the order.** The 10 Ω resistor shares the inner group's branch current. It does not share both terminal nodes with either 90 Ω or 45 Ω.
:::

sections.title: Kirchhoff examples: derive the signs and solve both supplied networks
sections.search:
Kirchhoff examples: derive the signs and solve both supplied networks

**Source correction — primary p. 66.** Different independent loops do not have to use the same traversal direction. Each loop can use either direction. Keep the signs consistent within that traversal. Reversing one complete loop equation multiplies it by −1 without changing the physical solution.

**Independent equations.** Repeating the junction equation at both ends of the same branches does not create new information. The outer loop is a combination of the two inner loops in the source example. Use enough independent equations for the unknown branch currents.

{{figure:m7-main:69|The primary single-loop circuit. A negative current reverses the displayed clockwise arrow.}}

:::example Primary single loop with opposing $6\,\mathrm{V}$ and $12\,\mathrm{V}$ batteries
**Source:** Primary p. 69. Assume clockwise current, as drawn. The resistors are 8 Ω and 10 Ω.

1. Traverse the top source from negative to positive: $+ 6\,\mathrm{V}$.
2. Traverse the 8 Ω resistor with the assumed current: −8I.
3. Traverse the bottom source from positive to negative: $- 12\,\mathrm{V}$.
4. Traverse the 10 Ω resistor with the assumed current: −10I.
5. Set the sum to zero: $6 - 8 I - 12 - 10 I = 0$.
6. Solve $- 6 - 18 I = 0$, giving $I = - \frac{1}{3} A$.

**Interpretation.** The actual current is $0.3333\,\mathrm{A}$ counterclockwise. The negative answer corrects the initial arrow; it does not invalidate Kirchhoff's rules.
:::

{{figure:m7-dyn:15|The separate companion two-loop network. Its component values differ from the primary network.}}

:::example Companion two-loop circuit: full elimination and voltage recovery
**Sources:** Companion pp. 14–16. **Given arrows:** $I_{1}$ rises through 2 Ω, $I_{2}$ rises through the 1 Ω and 3 Ω branch, and $I_{3}$ falls through 5 Ω. Sources are $16\,\mathrm{V}$ and $6\,\mathrm{V}$.

1. Write KCL at the upper node: $I_{3} = I_{1} + I_{2}$.
2. Write the left loop: $16 - 2 I_{1} - 5 I_{3} = 0$.
3. Write the right loop: $5 I_{3} + I_{2} + 3 I_{2} - 6 = 0$.
4. Substitute $I_{3} = I_{1} + I_{2}$ and collect terms.

$$\begin{aligned}
7I_1+5I_2&=16,\\
5I_1+9I_2&=6.
\end{aligned}$$

5. Multiply the first equation by 5 and the second by 7. Subtract the second from the first.

$$\begin{aligned}
35I_1+25I_2&=80,\\
35I_1+63I_2&=42,\\
-38I_2&=38\Rightarrow I_2=-1\ \mathrm A.
\end{aligned}$$

6. Back-substitute: $7 I_{1} + 5 \left( - 1 \right) = 16$, so $I_{1} = 3\,\mathrm{A}$.
7. Recover $I_{3} = 3 + \left( - 1 \right) = 2\,\mathrm{A}$ and $I_{4} = I_{2} = - 1\,\mathrm{A}$.
8. Calculate voltage-drop magnitudes: $6\,\mathrm{V}$ across 2 Ω; $1\,\mathrm{V}$ across 1 Ω; $10\,\mathrm{V}$ across 5 Ω; $3\,\mathrm{V}$ across 3 Ω.

**Checks.** Left loop: $16 - 6 - 10 = 0$. Right equation: $10 - 1 - 3 - 6 = 0$. $I_{2}$ and $I_{4}$ actually flow downward. Source power also balances: the $16\,\mathrm{V}$ source supplies $48\,\mathrm{W}$, the $6\,\mathrm{V}$ source absorbs $6\,\mathrm{W}$, and resistors dissipate $42\,\mathrm{W}$.
:::

sections.title: RC circuits: complete logarithms, limits, and switching checks
sections.search:
RC circuits: complete logarithms, limits, and switching checks

:::derivation Discharge from the differential equation to the time formula
**Sources:** Primary pp. 77–79. Let q be the charge remaining on the initially positive plate. The discharge-current magnitude is $- \frac{dq}{dt}$.

1. Use the loop equation $R \left( \frac{dq}{dt} \right) + \frac{q}{C} = 0$ under this charge convention.
2. Separate variables: $\frac{dq}{q} = - \frac{dt}{\left( RC \right)}$.
3. Integrate from $Q_{0}$ to q(t) and from 0 to t.
4. Exponentiate, divide by C for voltage, then isolate time when needed.

$$\ln\frac{q}{Q_0}=-\frac{t}{RC}
\Rightarrow q=Q_0e^{-t/RC},
\qquad V_C=V_0e^{-t/RC},
\qquad t=RC\ln\frac{V_0}{V_C}.$$

The logarithm uses a dimensionless ratio. For a decay fraction $f = \frac{V_{C}}{V_{0}}$, use $0 < f \le 1$. Reaching exactly zero takes infinite time in the ideal exponential model.
:::

:::example The source's $35\,\mathrm{\mu F}$, 120 Ω discharge problem
**Source:** Primary p. 79. **Find:** Time to fall to 10% of the initial voltage.

1. Convert $C = 35 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F}$.
2. Calculate $\tau = RC = 120 \left( 35 \times 10^{-6} \right) = 0.00420\,\mathrm{s}$.
3. Set $\frac{V_{C}}{V_{0}} = 0.10$, not 10.
4. Take logarithms: $\ln \left( 0.10 \right) = - \frac{t}{0.00420}$.
5. Solve $t = - 0.00420 \ln \left( 0.10 \right) = 0.00967086\,\mathrm{s} = 9.67\,\mathrm{ms}$.

**Check.** Ten percent remaining requires about 2.303 time constants. The initial voltage cancels because the question specifies a fraction.
:::

**Initial and final conditions.** An initially uncharged capacitor has $V_{C} \left( 0 \right) = 0$ and initially behaves as a zero-voltage element in the charging circuit. At DC steady state, its current tends to zero. A precharged capacitor is not initially a zero-voltage element. Use $V_{C} \left( t \right) = V_{f} + \left( V_{\mathrm{initial}} - V_{f} \right) \exp \left( - \frac{t}{\tau} \right)$ when the initial voltage is nonzero.

**Timing applications.** Wipers, traffic-light timers, camera flashes, and pacemaker timing circuits use charging or discharging intervals. The elementary RC model explains a time scale; it does not represent every control function inside those devices.
